Diffusion of Oxygen Through Activated
Sludge Flocs: Experimental Measurement,
Modeling, and Implications for Simultaneous
Nitriﬁcation and Denitriﬁcation
Glen T. Daigger1*, Craig D. Adams2, Holley Kaempfer Steller3
ABSTRACT:
Diffusion of dissolved oxygen through activated sludge ﬂocs
was studied, as it represents a potential mechanism for simultaneous nitri-
ﬁcation and denitriﬁcation in activated sludge systems. Dissolved oxygen
proﬁles through six ﬂoc particles collected at different times from a full-scale
activated sludge plant demonstrated that that the dissolved oxygen con-
centration declines through all ﬂoc particles. For larger ﬂoc particles (2-mm
diameter and greater), the dissolved oxygen concentration reached near-zero
values at depths depending on process operating conditions. A mathematical
model based on diffusion of dissolved oxygen, organic substrate (methanol),
ammonia, nitrite, and nitrate through a spherical ﬂoc and consumption of
dissolved oxygen by heterotrophs and autotrophs accurately predicted
the dissolved oxygen proﬁle and required adjustment of only one model
parameter—the concentration of heterotrophs. A different dissolved oxygen
decline pattern was exhibited for the smaller ﬂoc particles characterized,
with the dissolved oxygen reaching a non-zero plateau toward the center
of the ﬂoc. This pattern was not reproduced with the mathematical model
developed and suggests that additional mechanisms are responsible for the
transport of dissolved oxygen into the center of these ﬂocs. Implications
of these results regarding the occurrence of simultaneous nitriﬁcation and
denitriﬁcation include consideration of the factors that affect ﬂoc size and
distribution (simultaneous nitriﬁcation and denitriﬁcation is maximized with
largerﬂoc particles), couplingof the InternationalWaterAssociation (London)
activated models to predict activated sludge composition with diffusion
models to consider intraﬂoc effects, and the effects of substrate diffusion
on the apparent half-saturation constant for various substrates in activated
sludge systems. Water Environ. Res., 79, 375 (2007).
KEYWORDS:
activated sludge, biological nutrient removal, nitriﬁcation,
denitriﬁcation, simultaneous, diffusion, ﬂocs.

Introduction
Simultaneous nitriﬁcation and denitriﬁcation is a well-known phe-
nomenon in biological nutrient removal activated sludge systems.
As described in literature (Daigger and Littleton, 2000; Littleton,
2001, 2002; Littleton, Daigger, and Strom, 2003; Littleton, Daigger,
Strom, and Cowan, 2003), several mechanisms can be responsible
for its occurrence, but the two most likely are the following:
(1) Bioreactor macroenvironment. Anoxic and/or anaerobic zones
may develop within the bioreactor, as a result of the mixing
pattern caused, for example, by the oxygen transfer device.
(2) Floc microenvironment. Anoxic and/or anaerobic zones may
develop inside the activated sludge ﬂocs.
Diffusion of substrates through activated sludge ﬂocs is a well-
established phenomenon (Atkinson and Davies, 1974; Bakti, 1992;
Beneﬁeld and Molz, 1984; Kossen, 1979; Matson and Characklis,
1976). This phenomenon is accounted for in the popular Inter-
national Water Association (IWA) (London) activated sludge
models (ASMs), as a result of the half-saturation constants in the
Monod functions used in the microorganism growth rate expres-
sions for heterotrophs for dissolved oxygen and nitrate (O’Shaug-
nessey et al., 1998). With proper choice of these model parameters,
the IWA models can be tuned to account for simultaneous nitri-
ﬁcation and denitriﬁcation occurring in full-scale activated sludge
systems (Cinar et al., 1998; Daigger and Littleton, 2000). However,
it is desirable to better characterize this phenomenon so that predic-
tive models can be developed. This objective provided the moti-
vation for this research.
In this research, a method for measuring dissolved oxygen pro-
ﬁles through activated sludge ﬂocs was developed and used to test a
mathematical model for dissolved oxygen diffusion and use through
activated sludge ﬂocs. Some implications of these results relative to
the modeling of simultaneous nitriﬁcation and denitriﬁcation in
activated sludge systems are subsequently addressed.
Materials and Methods
Development
of
Mathematical
Model.
A
mathematical
model for the diffusion and metabolism of dissolved oxygen,
methanol, ammonia, nitrite, and nitrate through an activated sludge
ﬂoc was developed in spherical coordinates. The reactions incor-
porated to the model include the following:
(1) Aerobic growth of heterotrophs on dissolved organic matter
(methanol),
(2) Aerobic growth of ammonia-oxidizing autotrophs,
(3) Aerobic growth of nitrite-oxidizing autotrophs,
(4) Anoxic growth of heterotrophs using nitrate as a terminal
electron acceptor,
(5) Anoxic growth of heterotrophs using nitrite as a terminal
electron acceptor,

(6) Aerobic decay of heterotrophs,
(7) Anoxic decay of heterotrophs using nitrate as a terminal
electron acceptor, and
(8) Anoxic decay of heterotrophs using nitrite as a terminal electron

Ammonia- and nitrite-oxidizer decay, under both aerobic and
anoxic conditions, was omitted to simplify the model. Table 1
summarizes the kinetics and stoichiometry for the model in matrix
format, while Table 2 presents values of the kinetic, stroichiometric,
and diffusion parameters. Model parameters were largely taken from
Bakti and Dick (1992), as described in Steller (2003). Model
stoichiometry was developed based on microbial thermodynamics
(Steller, 2003). Floc particles are assumed to be spherical, and
boundary layer effects are considered to be negligible.
The model was implemented using the Scientist software pro-
gram (MicroMath, Salt Lake City, Utah) as a system of simulta-
neously solved ﬁrst-order ordinary differential equation according

The error-controlled Runge-Kutta numerical method was used
to solve the model. Only the aerobic (dissolved oxygen available)
portion of the model was tested experimentally, as data on only
the dissolved oxygen proﬁle through activated sludge ﬂocs were
obtained. The model was developed after Bakti (Bakti, 1988; Bakti
and Dick, 1992). Further details are available in Steller (2003).

Experimental Apparatus.
Dissolved Oxygen Microprobes
and Micromanipulator.
Dissolved oxygen microprobes manufac-
tured by Unisense (Unisence ApS, Science Park Aarhus, Denmark)
were used to measure dissolved oxygen proﬁles through activated
sludge particles, as illustrated in Figure 1. The microprobe is a
Clark-type electrode with a guard electrode. Probes with tip diam-
eters between 10 and 40 lm were used in this research. The 90%
response time for the probe ranged from 0.1 to 20 seconds, and its
detection limit was 0.003 mg/L, as reported by the manufacturer.
The stirring sensitivity is less than 1% difference. Electrical in-
terferences were signiﬁcant and were overcome using a grounding
wire from a grounded source directly into the solution being
measured. Current from the electrode was measured using a fast-
response (50 milliseconds for 90% response time) Model PA2000
picoammeter (Unisense) and was further recorded using Labview
data
acquisition
software
(National
Instruments
Corporation,
Austin, Texas). The data were subsequently exported to Microsoft
Excel for subsequent analysis (Microsoft Corporation, Bellevue,
Washington). The microprobe was moved through the activated
sludge ﬂoc using a micromanipulator (Unisense) capable of moving
the probe by as little as 5-lm increments.
Reactor Design.
A reactor was constructed to trap activated
sludge ﬂocs and to recirculate solution with deﬁned properties past
the ﬂoc to maintain a uniform environment. Figure 2 illustrates the
reactor, which consisted of a bulk chamber (3.8-L volume, mixed to
provide uniform bulk properties, i.e., dissolved oxygen) and a ﬂoc-
capture chamber (127 mL), where the solution was continuously
passed by a ﬂoc particle captured on a monoﬁlament grid, as shown
in Figure 3. Dissolved oxygen in the bulk chamber was measured

using two Corning model 317 probes (Corning, Inc., Corning, New
York). Aeration was manipulated to achieve the desired bulk dis-
solved oxygen. A peristaltic pump was used to recirculate the bulk
solution at a ﬂowrate of 5.1 mL/min, providing a ﬂow velocity of
0.8 cm/min in the ﬂoc chamber to maintain constant conditions for
the trapped ﬂoc particle. The hydraulic residence time in the ﬂoc
capture chamber was 25 minutes. Recirculation was maintained for
50 minutes before dissolved oxygen proﬁles were measured. This
time was based on the time required for diffusion of oxygen through
the largest ﬂoc particles studied (i.e., 4 mm) using the smallest
diffusion coefﬁcient reported in the literature (Steller, 2003), with
an additional safety factor of three. The actual size of the ﬂoc
particles that were proﬁled ranged from 0.25 to 3 mm. Floc particles
were captured with a 1-mL pipette from a seed sample collected
from the Southeast Rolla (Missouri) Wastewater Treatment Plant
and gently placed onto the monoﬁlament grid. A 1-mL sample was
transferred. The Southeast Rolla Wastewater Treatment Plant is an
extended aeration activated sludge plant, with no primary clariﬁ-
cation, that treats predominantly municipal wastewater. After steady-
state conditions were achieved, the microprobe was moved through
the captured ﬂoc at increments of either 0.005 or 0.01 mm in the
downward direction to collect proﬁle data. The reactor temperature
was maintained at 228C (1/228C). Figure 4 provides a photograph of
the entire experimental apparatus.
Feed Solution.
Table 4 summarizes the components of the syn-
thetic solution used. The concentrations of methanol and ammonia-
nitrogen were varied, depending on experimental objectives. Feed
solution was prepared daily using prepared stock solutions and
diluting with tap water to achieve the desired chemical oxygen
demand (COD) and nitrogen concentrations. The concentrations of
constituents were sufﬁciently high to be in excess of the biosyn-
thetic requirements for all COD concentrations used. Biodegrada-
tion and volatilization of methanol from the feed solution were
conﬁrmed to be negligible by COD measurements of freshly pre-
pared feed solution and solutions after 1 day, which conﬁrmed that
methanol loss was less than 4%.
Analytical Methods.
The COD, ammonia, nitrate, and nitrite
were measured with a Hach DR/2010 (Hach Company, Loveland,
Colorado) using methods 8000, 10031, 10020, and 8507, respec-
tively. Total and volatile suspended solids were measured using
Standard Methods 2540D and 2540E, respectively (APHA et al.,
1995).
Results
Initial intraﬂoc dissolved oxygen proﬁles developed in ﬂoc
particles from the Southeast Rolla Wastewater Treatment Plant
demonstrated that the dissolved oxygen proﬁle through the ﬂoc
depended on external dissolved oxygen concentration, among other
factors, and that the dissolved oxygen inside of the ﬂoc would
approach zero when the bulk (or external) dissolved oxygen con-
centration was sufﬁciently low (data not shown). The results also
demonstrated that insertion of the probe created a channel that
resulted in a different dissolved oxygen proﬁle when the probe was
withdrawn than when it was inserted. The dissolved oxygen proﬁle
when the probe was subsequently reinserted was also different than
for the ﬁrst insertion. Thus, only proﬁles from the ﬁrst insertion are
reported here. For more details, see Steller (2003).
Collection of reliable dissolved oxygen proﬁles proved to be
quite tedious. Consequently, six proﬁles from four activated sludge
samples (referred to as samples A through D) collected at distinctly
different times were measured. For activated sludge samples A and
B, dissolved oxygen proﬁles for two different ﬂoc particles were
obtained, while, for samples C and D, only one ﬂoc particle from
each activated sludge sample was proﬁled. For samples A and B,
the mathematical model was calibrated to one dissolved oxygen
proﬁle, and the calibrated model was then used to predict the proﬁle
for the other ﬂoc particle (that is, one ﬂoc was used for model
calibration, while the other was used for model veriﬁcation). The
sample A and B models were subsequently compared with the
sample C and D results. Default model parameters were used for all
but the bulk dissolved oxygen, methanol, and ammonia concentra-

approximately 0.9 mm, which corresponds to a ﬂoc volume of
approximately 12%, with near-zero dissolved oxygen based on the
spherical ﬂoc particle assumption. The ﬁt of the experimental data

Figure 7 shows the results for the ﬁrst sample B ﬂoc particle,
which has a 2.5-mm diameter. The dissolved oxygen concentration
decreased from the bulk dissolved oxygen concentration of 2.9 mg/
L to near zero, at a depth of approximately 0.3 mm, indicating that
approximately 31% of the ﬂoc volume had a near-zero dissolved
oxygen concentration based on the spherical ﬂoc particle assump-
tion. As shown in Figure 7, the model could be ﬁt to the model by
adjusting the heterotroph concentration to 1500 mg/L (versus 200
mg/L for sample A) and that an excellent ﬁt could be achieved.
The R2 for the calibrated model was 99.3%. Figure 8 shows a pro-
ﬁle for the second ﬂoc particle (1-mm diameter) from sample B,
which was examined at a bulk dissolved oxygen concentration of
5.8 mg/L. In this case, the measured dissolved oxygen proﬁle exhib-
ited a different shape than observed with the three previous proﬁles
(Figures 5 to 7) and tended to level out at a depth of approximately
0.4 mm. The observed rate of dissolved oxygen depletion was
intermediate between the model predictions based on the hetero-
troph concentrations determined for samples A and B. The R2 for
this ﬂoc particle compared with the sample B model was 88.6%, but
exhibited an obvious lack of ﬁt.
Figures 9 and 10 show the dissolved oxygen proﬁles for the
sample C and D particles. The sample C particle (Figure 9) was 1.1
mm in diameter, and the bulk dissolved oxygen concentration was
3.5 mg/L, while the sample D particle was 4 mm in diameter, and
the bulk dissolved oxygen concentration was 6.1 mg/L. The sample
C ﬂoc particle showed a dissolved oxygen proﬁle similar to that
from validation run from sample B—declining at a rate intermediate
between the predicted values based on the calibrated models from
samples A and B and reaching a plateau value approximately 0.35
mm into the ﬂoc particle. In contrast, the larger sample D ﬂoc
particle initially showed a decline in dissolved oxygen concentra-
tion that was well predicted by the model results using the sample A
calibration, but diverged signiﬁcantly at approximately 0.7 mm in
depth, even though a near-zero dissolved oxygen concentration was
reached at approximately 1.6 mm into the ﬂoc particle.

Discussion
Similar dissolved oxygen proﬁles are observed for larger ﬂoc
particles (2-mm diameter and larger), as illustrated in Figures 5 to
7 and 10, compared with the smaller ﬂocs (approximately 1-mm
diameter), as illustrated in Figures 8 and 9. For the larger ﬂocs, the
dissolved oxygen decreased regularly with depth and reached near-
zero values. The penetration depth for dissolved oxygen depended
on the external dissolved oxygen and the activity of the activated
sludge ﬂoc (as represented in the concentration of heterotrophs in
the calibrated model). The exception to this general trend is for the
sample D ﬂoc particle, which exhibited this behavior for the outer
portion of the activated sludge ﬂoc, but departed for the inner
portion. It is uncertain why this divergence occurred, but it could
have been a result of measurement difﬁculty, nonhomogeneity for
the ﬂoc particle, or divergence from the assumption of a spherical
ﬂoc particle. Li and Bishop (2004) observed similar dissolved
oxygen proﬁles in ﬂoc particles with diameters greater than 1 mm
from two wastewater treatment plants in Cincinnati, Ohio. In con-
trast, for the smaller ﬂoc particles (Figures 8 and 9), the dissolved
oxygen decreased with depth into the ﬂoc particle, but tended to
plateau at nonzero dissolved oxygen levels at the middle of the ﬂoc
particle. The external dissolved oxygen was relatively high for both
of these proﬁles (5.8 mg/L for Figure 8 and 3.5 mg/L for Figure 9),
which may help to explain this behavior. Alternatively, these results
may represent a difference in the structure and/or density of smaller
versus larger ﬂoc particles. It is also possible that insertion of the
dissolved oxygen microprobe disrupted the ﬂoc structure of the
smaller particles (the probe was of ﬁxed dimensions and, conse-
quently, could disrupt smaller ﬂocs to a greater extent than larger
ﬂocs), resulting in nonrepresentative dissolved oxygen proﬁle
measurements.
The mathematical model was able to characterize the dissolved
oxygen proﬁle through the larger ﬂoc particles quite well, by only
adjusting the concentration of heterotrophs (Figures 5 to 7). For
sample A, the model calibrated to the ﬁrst ﬂoc particle (Figure 5)
predicted the dissolved oxygen proﬁle through the second ﬂoc
particle (Figure 6) quite well. The model also characterized the
dissolved oxygen proﬁle through the ﬁrst ﬂoc particle from sample
B, although the heterotroph concentration had to be adjusted. This is
reasonable, as the two samples were taken at different times from
the full-scale wastewater treatment plant, and operating conditions
could well have been quite different for the two samples. However,
the proﬁles for the smaller ﬂoc particles (Figures 8 and 9) could not
be characterized using the model. Efforts to adjust model param-
eters to allow the model to predict a leveling-off of the dissolved
oxygen proﬁle in the interior of the ﬂoc particle were unsuccessful
(Steller, 2003).

The potential that different behaviors will be observed for ﬂoc
particles of different sizes is signiﬁcant, because the ﬂoc size in acti-
vated sludge systems is not uniform. Rather, a distribution of par-
ticle sizes exists (Jorand et al., 1995; Li and Ganczarczyk, 1991),
with the speciﬁc distribution depending on a number of biological,
chemical, and physical factors (Bouyer et al., 2001; Govoreanu
et al., 2004; Li and Ganczarczyk, 1993; Wilen, 1999). For example,
turbulence in the aeration basin can lead to shear that reduces par-
ticle size, while ﬂocculation will increase particle sizes (Parker
et al., 1971). A complete analysis of intraﬂoc effects on the behavior
of an activated sludge process would require consideration of the
distribution of ﬂoc particle sizes.
It is encouraging that model calibration required only adjustment
of the heterotroph concentration. The sensitivity analysis (Table 3)
indicated that the model was most sensitive to ﬂoc surface con-
centrations, followed by diffusivities for the diffusing species, and
then kinetic parameters (maximum speciﬁc rates and half-velocity
coefﬁcients). For example, of the 14 parameters found to affect
model response to the greatest extent (high sensitivity), 9 were ﬂoc
surface concentrations, and 5 were diffusivities. Likewise, of the
29 parameters found to affect model response moderately (moderate
sensitivity), 14 were surface concentrations, 2 were diffusivities,
and 12 were kinetic parameters. When modeling an actual operating
system using, for example, one of the IWA activated sludge models,
many of these constituents and parameters, including the compo-
sition of the biomass, will be known. Thus, a diffusion model can
be used to predict phenomena occurring inside the ﬂoc particles,
assuming that values of the diffusivities are accurately known. In
fact, the respiration rate predicted by the ASM for the operating
conditions experienced can be used, with a dispersion model, to
determine whether, for a particular operating bulk dissolved oxygen
concentration, the activated sludge ﬂoc will remain fully aerobic or
whether an oxygen-deﬁcient inner portion will develop where
denitriﬁcation can occur. Thus, one can envision a coupling of the
ASM with an intraﬂoc diffusion model to characterize the intraﬂoc
mechanism for simultaneous nitriﬁcation and denitriﬁcation.
The proﬁles presented in Figures 5 to 10 clearly illustrate that
the concentrations of various substrates experienced by bacteria in
activated sludge ﬂocs can vary signiﬁcantly from the bulk con-
centration. This requires a reinterpretation of the meaning of half-
saturation coefﬁcients for activated sludge systems. For example,
it is possible that the observed half-saturation value for dissolved
oxygen reﬂects the bulk dissolved oxygen needed to cause oxygen
to fully penetrate the ﬂoc particle, rather than the actual effect of
dissolved oxygen on the metabolism of the bacteria. Further, this
dissolved oxygen will depend on a number of factors, including the
respiration rate for the mixed liquor and ﬂoc particle size (and its
distribution). Floc diffusion models can be used to estimate these

Summary and Conclusions
In summary, an intraﬂoc diffusion model was developed to
predict dissolved oxygen proﬁles through activated sludge ﬂocs.
This model was then compared with activated sludge ﬂoc dissolved
oxygen proﬁles measured with a dissolved oxygen microprobe.
For large ﬂoc particles (approximately 2-mm diameter or greater),
a regular dissolved oxygen proﬁle was observed that was
well-predicted by the developed model. Model calibration was
accomplished by adjusting a single model parameter—the concen-
tration of heterotrophs. This concentration varied from one activated
sludge sample to another, but was consistent from one ﬂoc particle
to another for a speciﬁc activated sludge sample. The proﬁles for
the larger ﬂoc particles also clearly demonstrated that dissolved-
oxygen-deﬁcient zones can form in activated sludge ﬂocs. These are
locations where denitriﬁcation can occur.
The dissolved oxygen proﬁle through smaller ﬂoc particles
also showed a decline in dissolved oxygen, but with a leveling-off,
so that near-zero dissolved oxygen concentrations were not reached
at the center of the ﬂoc. The mathematical model could not be
adjusted to predict intraﬂoc dissolved oxygen proﬁles of this type.
Based on these results, the following can be concluded:
(1) The dissolved oxygen declines through activated sludge ﬂocs of
all sizes measured, so that the microorganisms in ﬂoc particles
will experience dissolved oxygen concentrations lower than the
bulk dissolved oxygen concentration. The decline in dissolved
oxygen concentration in the ﬂoc particle varies, depending on
both ﬂoc size and environmental conditions, so that the bulk
dissolved oxygen concentration, by itself, is not an accurate
indicator of the dissolved oxygen concentration that the
microorganisms in an activated sludge ﬂoc will experience.
(2) The dissolved oxygen proﬁle for the larger ﬂoc particles con-
sidered in this research declined and reached near-zero values at
depths depending on ﬂoc properties and operating conditions. It
is hypothesized that these near-zero zones within the ﬂoc can
provide an environment where denitriﬁcation can occur.
(3) The dissolved oxygen decline within larger ﬂoc particles (2-mm
diameter and greater) was accurately characterized using the
mathematical model developed. In this model, dissolved
oxygen, organic substrate (methanol), ammonia, nitrite, and
nitrate are transported by diffusion through a spherical particle,

and dissolved oxygen is consumed by oxidation of methanol by
heterotrophs and ammonia and nitrite by autotrophs.
(4) The developed mathematical model could be calibrated to the
dissolved oxygen proﬁles for the larger ﬂoc particles, by simply
adjusting the concentration of heterotrophs. For a given
activated sludge sample, the same model (same heterotroph
concentration) was able to accurately characterize the dissolved
oxygen proﬁle through two separate activated sludge ﬂocs.
However, different heterotroph concentrations were required to
characterize the dissolved oxygen proﬁle through large ﬂoc
particles through two sludge samples collected at different
times, representing two different operating conditions for the
full-scale activated sludge system.
(5) In contrast, for smaller ﬂoc particles (diameter of roughly 1 mm
and smaller) the dissolved oxygen decreased, but did not reach
near-zero values. Proﬁles of this shape could not be predicted
by the developed mathematical model. This suggests that
additional mechanisms are transporting dissolved oxygen into
the activated sludge ﬂoc.
These results are signiﬁcant relative to the occurrence of simul-
taneous nitriﬁcation and denitriﬁcation in activated sludge systems.
The distribution of ﬂoc sizes in activated sludge systems must be
considered in connection with the intraﬂoc denitriﬁcation mecha-
nism. Factors that increase the average ﬂoc size, especially the
proportion of large ﬂoc particles, will increase the potential that
intraﬂoc denitriﬁcation can occur. For operating systems, the
composition of biomass will be predicted by process mathematical
models, such as the IWA activated sludge models. This composi-
tion, with an intraﬂoc diffusion model, can be used to calculate
intraﬂoc dissolved oxygen proﬁles, to determine the bulk dissolved
oxygen concentration required at various points within the process,
to allow dissolved oxygen to decline to near-zero levels within
the ﬂoc, thereby allowing intraﬂoc denitriﬁcation to occur. These
results also suggest that apparent half-saturation constants for
various substrates reﬂect both the inherent effect of substrate
concentration on the activity of the microorganisms and the effects
of diffusion of that substrate through the activated sludge ﬂoc
particle. Consequently, the apparent half-saturation constants may
vary through the activated sludge process, depending on process
operating conditions and the resulting diffusion of that substrate into
the activated sludge ﬂoc.
